key_terms.meaning: A continuous-time voltage or current that varies smoothly with time
A sequence of discrete voltage levels representing binary bits
Measuring an analog signal at uniform intervals; rate must be ≥ 2× highest frequency (Nyquist rate)
Mapping each sampled amplitude to the nearest value in a finite set; introduces quantization noise
Number of bits transmitted per second, unit bps
Loss of signal power with distance, expressed in dB
Alteration of signal waveform due to bandwidth limits or non‑linearities
Random unwanted electrical fluctuations; measured as power spectral density
Ratio of signal power to noise power; SNR = P_signal ÷ P_noise, often expressed in dB
Frequency range of a channel (Hz) that can carry useful signal energy
Maximum symbol rate = 2 × bandwidth (symbols/s) for a noiseless channel
Maximum data rate C = B × log₂(1+SNR) bits/s, where B is bandwidth
Physical transmission paths such as twisted pair, coaxial cable, or optical fiber
Wireless transmission through air or space, e.g., radio, microwave, infrared, satellite
Mapping bits to voltage levels; examples: NRZ, Manchester, bipolar‑AMI
Binary 1 = high level, 0 = low level; no inherent clock
Each bit period contains a transition; 0 = high→low, 1 = low→high, provides clock
Carrier amplitude varies between two levels to represent 0 and 1
Carrier frequency shifts between two values for binary symbols
Carrier phase changes (e.g., 0°/180°) to encode bits
Divides channel bandwidth into non‑overlapping frequency slots for multiple signals
Allocates successive time slots to different data streams on the same channel
FDM applied to optical fiber using different light wavelengths
Expands a narrow‑band signal over a wide frequency band using a pseudo‑random code
Rate at which spreading code chips are transmitted, higher than data bit rate
Ratio of chip rate to data rate; indicates how much the signal is spread

takeaways: Digital data can be carried over analog media by sampling and quantization.
Attenuation, distortion and noise degrade signals; repeaters and equalizers mitigate them.
Maximum data rate is limited by bandwidth and SNR (Nyquist and Shannon formulas).
Guided media offer high capacity and low loss; unguided media provide mobility.
Line coding determines signal integrity and clock recovery on a digital link.
Modulation maps digital bits onto carrier wave parameters for long‑distance transmission.
Multiplexing efficiently shares a physical link among many users.
Spread spectrum improves security and resistance to interference.
bank_note: Some syllabi emphasize clear definitions, formula derivations and practical examples for long‑answer questions in this unit.

bank.q: Explain the process of converting an analog voice signal into a digital bit stream. Include sampling, quantization, and encoding steps.
outline: Define analog and digital signals
State Nyquist sampling theorem and required sampling rate
Describe quantization and its effect on signal quality
Mention PCM encoding and bit rate calculation

bank.q: State the Nyquist formula and the Shannon–Hartley capacity formula. Define each symbol used.
outline: Write Nyquist: C = 2B log₂ M
Write Shannon: C = B log₂(1+SNR)
Define B, C, M, SNR

bank.q: A 2 km twisted‑pair link has an attenuation of 2 dB/km and a bandwidth of 1 MHz. If the transmitter sends a signal with 0 dBm power and the receiver sensitivity is –80 dBm, determine whether the link can support a 10 Mbps NRZ transmission.
outline: Calculate total attenuation (2 dB/km × 2 km = 4 dB)
Find received power (0 dBm – 4 dB = –4 dBm)
Compare with sensitivity (–4 dBm > –80 dBm, link is feasible)
Check Nyquist limit: C = 2B = 2 MHz = 2 Mbps for binary NRZ; conclude 10 Mbps exceeds limit

bank.q: Design a simple line‑coding scheme for a 100 Mbps link that provides both DC balance and clock recovery. Explain why your scheme meets the requirements.
outline: Choose Manchester coding
Show transition in each bit period gives clock
Explain equal number of high and low levels gives DC balance
Mention bandwidth requirement (≈2× data rate)

bank.q: Compare Frequency Division Multiplexing (FDM) and Time Division Multiplexing (TDM) for a satellite communication system. Discuss bandwidth efficiency, latency, and implementation complexity.
outline: Define FDM and TDM
Calculate bandwidth usage for given number of channels
Explain latency impact of TDM slot waiting vs. FDM propagation
Discuss hardware complexity: filters for FDM, timing circuits for TDM
Conclude which is preferable under typical satellite constraints

bank.q: Assess the advantages and disadvantages of using spread‑spectrum techniques (e.g., DSSS) in a Wi‑Fi (802.11) network operating in a crowded urban environment.
outline: Explain DSSS principle and processing gain
List advantages: interference resistance, security, multipath mitigation
List disadvantages: lower spectral efficiency, higher power consumption
Relate to urban spectrum congestion and regulatory limits
Provide overall evaluation for Wi‑Fi deployment

bank.q: Describe the main types of guided media and their typical applications in Indian telecom networks.
outline: Twisted pair: telephone, broadband DSL
Coaxial cable: cable TV, older Ethernet
Optical fiber: high‑speed backbone, metro links

bank.q: A wireless link operates at 2.4 GHz with a bandwidth of 20 MHz and an average SNR of 30 dB. Using the Shannon formula, compute the theoretical maximum data rate.
outline: Convert SNR from dB to linear (10^(30/10) = 1000)
Apply C = B log₂(1+SNR) = 20 MHz × log₂(1001)
Calculate log₂(1001) ≈ 9.97 bits
Result ≈ 199 Mbps

bank.q: Explain how attenuation and dispersion affect signal integrity in an optical fiber link of 50 km. Suggest two mitigation techniques.
outline: Define attenuation (loss per km) and dispersion (pulse spreading)
Show impact on eye diagram and BER
Mitigation 1: Use optical amplifiers (EDFA) to compensate loss
Mitigation 2: Employ dispersion‑shifted fiber or dispersion compensation modules

bank.q: List three common modulation schemes used for digital data transmission over radio links and give one characteristic of each.
outline: ASK – simple amplitude variation, sensitive to noise
FSK – frequency shifts, more robust to amplitude noise
PSK – phase changes, high spectral efficiency

bank.q: For a TDM system with 8 users sharing a 1 Gbps link, calculate the slot duration for each user assuming equal bandwidth allocation.
outline: Total bit period = 1 / 1 Gbps = 1 ns
Slot per user = 8 ns (since 8 users)
Explain that each user gets 125 Mbps effective rate

bank.q: Discuss the trade‑offs between using NRZ and Manchester line coding in a high‑speed Ethernet (10 GbE) link.
outline: NRZ: lower bandwidth, no inherent clock, risk of baseline wander
Manchester: double bandwidth, built‑in clock, better synchronization
Impact on transceiver design, power consumption, and error performance
Conclusion on suitability for 10 GbE
